did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm opens by addressing the LORD as “my Rock”—a symbol of stability and protection—and asking him not to remain silent, because the worshiper fears being counted among those who go down to the pit.
Did you know? The worshiper describes both the sound of his pleas and the lifting of his hands toward “the inner sanctuary of your holiness,” meaning the LORD’s holy place.
Did you know? The worshiper asks not to be swept along with people who speak words of peace outwardly but harbor evil in their hearts.

Did you know? The request for repayment is expressed in several parallel phrases: “according to their deeds,” “according to the evil of their actions,” and “according to the work of their hands”—a measure-for-measure response based on what they have done.

Did you know? The reason given for the wicked’s punishment is that they do not understand the LORD’s works or the work of his hands; therefore, it is said of them that they will be torn down and not built up.
Did you know? At this point the psalm takes a turn: after a series of requests, thanksgiving appears because the worshiper declares that the LORD has heard the sound of his pleas.
Did you know? The LORD is described through two complementary images—“my strength” and “my shield”—and trust in him fills the worshiper’s heart with joy and leads him to praise in song.
Did you know? The prayer expands from the individual to the community: the LORD is the strength of his people and a stronghold of salvation for “his anointed one,” meaning the one he has anointed.
Did you know? The psalm ends with a prayer for the people, asking for salvation, blessing, guidance like a shepherd, and continual support—“forever.”
